Blue — removed from the accountsWhen other income does not cover the paycheck, expenses, and taxes, the needed amount is withdrawn from the 401(k), IRA, or Roth.

Taxes can make blue largerIf taxes are paid from retirement money, the lower blue amount can be higher than the paycheck because the withdrawal also includes tax.
Roth FirstUses Roth money first, then traditional accounts. Usually lowers taxable withdrawals early.
IRA / 401(k) FirstUses traditional retirement money first, then Roth. Taxable withdrawals may be higher early.
ProportionalSplits the paycheck across account types. Taxes and balances are spread between the accounts.

Refresh after changing any earlier page. Check the yearly table for tax spikes, large withdrawals, or a negative ending balance before printing or exporting.

2

Page 4 tax reminder + dynamic tax calculation

This tax reminder tells users that tax assumptions can change and should be reviewed.

The Retirement Chart includes taxes in the projection. When the user changes Roth conversion, filing status, state tax setting, income, pension, IRA withdrawal, or assumptions, the chart recalculates the tax effect.

Federal taxes

The calculator uses the federal tax settings shown in the tax area. The user can update the brackets and apply the changes.

State taxes

The user can choose taxed or exempt. When state tax is on, the projection includes state tax. When exempt is selected, state tax is removed.

Roth conversion taxes

When IRA money is converted to Roth, the calculator shows the tax cost and where that tax payment comes from.
3

Color meaning inside the calculator

The colors help users understand the chart quickly without reading every number.

Red: Traditional IRA / 401(k), expenses, or account money going down
Yellow: Roth IRA / Roth conversion money
Green: paycheck, usable income, or money left over
Orange: employer pension or large expense category
Blue: Social Security or utility-style category
Cyan: rental / other income
Black: federal taxes or credit/debt category
Gray: state taxes or miscellaneous items

Page 2: Income + Expenses

This page collects the starting numbers: income, expenses, savings, 401(k), Roth, and monthly categories. The block chart makes the budget visual immediately.

What loads forward

Monthly income, expenses, 401(k), Roth, savings, and inflation-adjusted spending.

Why it matters

Later pages use these values to estimate growth, taxes, retirement income, and whether retirement expenses are covered.
The green block is total monthly income. The blocks underneath show expenses and savings by category.

Page 3: 401(k), IRA, and Roth growth

This chart shows red IRA/401(k), yellow Roth IRA, and tax/paycheck amounts together.

The 401(k), IRA, and Roth page helps the user test retirement age, contributions, growth rate, and Roth balances. The final year values become the starting point for the retirement projection.

Red grows taxable retirement money

Traditional IRA and 401(k) balances may grow large, but withdrawals may create taxes later.

Yellow grows Roth money

Roth money is separated so users can compare Roth growth against traditional retirement money.

The ending amount carries forward

The final IRA/401(k) and Roth balances load into the Retirement Chart.

7

Slider range: increase or decrease the max

The slider controls let users make fast changes and then fine-tune. If the max is too small, increase the range. If the slider is too wide, decrease the range for better control.

Increase range

Use this for a bigger paycheck, pension, IRA, Roth conversion, Social Security, or contribution amount.

Decrease range

Use this when the range is too large and small changes are hard to make.
The range buttons make phone use easier and make the slider more accurate.
8

Roth conversion: why it can help

A Roth conversion moves money from a Traditional IRA or 401(k) into a Roth account. The user may pay taxes now so more money can sit in the Roth side for future planning.

Possible benefit

It may create more Roth money later and may reduce how much taxable IRA money remains in future years.

Tradeoff

The conversion can create a tax bill now. That is why the calculator shows different ways to pay the taxes.
The calculator shows possible outcomes only. The user decides what to do and should talk with a financial advisor or tax professional.
The tax payment choice changes which account loses money when the tax bill is paid.
9

How the Roth tax buttons work

💵 Pay from Cash / Savings
Taxes come from money outside retirement accounts. The full conversion can stay in Roth.
🔴 Pay from Traditional IRA
The IRA pays the tax too, so the IRA balance drops more.
🟡 Pay from Roth
The Roth receives the conversion, then pays the tax. This reduces Roth money.
This moving demo starts automatically. It shows the idea of account values changing when the tax payment method changes.
10

Tax brackets and assumptions

Tax brackets can be edited and applied to the calculator.
Other assumptions control slider maximums and planning limits.

These settings are included because taxes, state rules, contribution limits, and assumptions can change. The calculator lets the user update assumptions, but it does not replace a professional tax review.

11

Page 5: Retirement Expenses

The selected retirement year loads the projected income for that year.

This page answers: “In this retirement year, do I have enough monthly income to cover my expenses?”

Year selector

The user chooses a retirement year. That year pulls projected income from the Retirement Chart.

Income versus expenses

The page compares usable monthly income against inflation-adjusted expenses.

Result

The bottom message tells the user if they are under budget or short for that month.
Expenses can be adjusted by category.
The block chart makes the retirement budget easy to understand visually.
✓

Final plain-English explanation

This calculator helps users test retirement possibilities. It estimates taxes, retirement funds, Roth conversions, income, expenses, and inflation using the numbers entered by the user. It does not tell the user what to invest in and does not make financial decisions for them.

The user is responsible for their own choices. Before investing, converting to Roth, changing retirement contributions, or making tax decisions, they should talk with a qualified financial advisor or tax professional.
